But this was still a dazzling occasion at the Parc des Princes, where the champions of France and Spain played out a light, open, frictionless, exhibition-style game of football. quietus.title: Beyond The Pleasuredome: Frankie Goes To Hollywood’s Liverpool 40 Years On
quietus.description: Wyndham Wallace looks at the oft-neglected follow-up to FGTH's debut, Liverpool which was released in 1986 Compare and contrast: "The world is my oyster," the opening words to Frankie Goes To Hollywood's debut album, 1984's Welcome To The Pleasuredome. Delivered by Holly Johnson in the flippant style of a cartoon villain, a cackling laugh in their wake. "I'm looking for something and I don't know what it is," the last words to Frankie Goes To Hollywood's second and final album, 1986's Liverpool. Delivered by Holly Johnson in the style of a man running on empty, almost bereft of hope. What a difference a couple of years can make. Frankie Goes To Hollywood first hit the top of the UK charts…

quietus.title: An Evergreen Lodestar of all that is Abominable: How Reign in Blood Changed Metal
quietus.description: Ian Winwood looks back 40 years to his first contact with an imperial and imperious Slayer and their third album's "frenzied scream of wall-eyed mayhem" On the weekend before Christmas, in 2020, I sent a friend a text message comprised of just three words. It read: Epidemic. Permanent disease. I had no doubt that my old familiar would recognise the bulletin as being a snippet of a lyric from Reign In Blood, by Slayer. Thirty-four years earlier, while listening for the first time to an import edition of the album dispatched by post from Shades Records, in Soho, the two of us had been forever conjoined by the fiercest musical experience of our teenage lives. We’d stood transfixed in the…

quietus.title: Fisherman’s Blues: the Damning Indictment cast by All Rivers Spill Their Stories To The Sea
quietus.description: Claire Sawers talks to director Jeanie Finlay about her hard-hitting, emotionally resonant documentary about toxic pollution of UK waters, which doubles as love letter to the north east Stan Rennie takes a tea break, by Jeanie Finlay “I’m sick as a chip”, says Stan Rennie. He’s dressed in shiny orange fisherman’s bibs and lifejacket, sat aboard his blue and white boat, the Sarah Lynn, on the waters around Hartlepool. That particular Northernism nails his beyond fed up feeling. We’d say ‘seek’ in Scots. Flattened by the injustice of his situation and we’re right there with him. It’s at the end of the documentary All Rivers Spill Their Stories To The Sea and we’re glimpsing a rare moment of…

And even then, not everything is getting captured. Think how many formalised music-making sessions are happening somewhere, as I write and you read. The participants are likely finding their feet and letting off steam, not attempting to create something for public consumption. But what if someone involved realises the…

We’re not making new tracks,” insists Watson. For Mallinder, “we don’t want to be a tribute band. The end’s going to stagger a little bit, because we can’t stop at every territory within that period, but it will end. “It’s for Richard really,” he continues, namechecking the permanently absent third member of their gang. “I don’t want to take the piss, it has to be a finite thing.” The Cabs are…

aquariumdrunkard.title: Fela Kuti & Africa ’70 :: Live in Berlin (Berliner Jazztage, 1978)
aquariumdrunkard.description: No retreat. No surrender. Filmed at the Berliner Jazztage on November 4, 1978, with Tony Allen still at the kit, this 87-minute document captures Fela Kuti and Africa ’70 at the end of their Herculean run. Unearthed decades later, the tapes capture the collective’s internal chemistry intact at the very moment its future was set to fracture.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Introducing Radio Free Aquarium Drunkard: Longform Listening. Worldwide. 24/7.
aquariumdrunkard.description: A Continuous Broadcast from Aquarium Drunkard. Hand-curated. No playlists. Nothing to scroll. Nothing random. Everything intentional. Transmitting from the hills of Northeast Los Angeles, Radio Free Aquarium Drunkard is a free, always-on radio station. Press play and you're tuned in to what's on the air right now, alongside everyone else. The broadcast continues and tracks advance whether or not you're listening. The app is free, but requires an active Apple Music subscription. James Barnes is the architect. Justin Gage is the selector.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Twin Peaks: Fire Walk With Me (Soundtrack, Angelo Badalamenti)

The soundtrack to David Lynch’s Twin Peaks: Fire Walk with Me seems to exist just beyond all three, somewhere between the last light and whatever waits after dark.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Booker Stardrum :: The Aquarium Drunkard Interview
aquariumdrunkard.description: Jazz grip. Booker Stardrum’s work spans solo recordings, electronic experiments, and collective improvisation. In 2026, he’s released his fourth solo album, Close-up On The Outside , alongside new records with Play Time, OOPS!, Silk Fence, and SML. We spoke with Stardrum about his compositional process and the challenges and possibilities of working across so many different musical settings.

aquariumdrunkard.title: RFAD :: October 2026
aquariumdrunkard.description: Freeform transmissions from Radio Free Aquarium Drunkard on dublab. Airing every third Sunday of the month, RFAD on dublab features the pairing of Tyler Wilcox’s Doom and Gloom from the Tomb and Chad DePasquale’s New Happy Gathering. This month, Tyler kicks things off with a grab-bag of folk jazz and dream pop; Chad follows it up with an hour of Senegalese folk, Malian funk, Malaysian jazz, Filipino psych & more. Sunday, 4-6pm PT.

aquariumdrunkard.title: PAINT :: Whip of an Ear
aquariumdrunkard.description: No one is making music quite like PAINT, the project of musician and Allah-Las guitarist Pedrum Siadatian. If a song title can be prophetic, it's "Illusion of Voice" here, in which the vocals of real and hypothetical cast of ensemble characters and collaborators weave through a shadowy labyrinth full of twists of surrealistic transparency. From police blotter audio soundscapes to warbled poetry reads, fourth record Whip of an Ear is an obtusely captivating listen and one of the prolific musician's best offerings yet.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Piero Umiliani :: Il Corpo
aquariumdrunkard.description: Piero Umiliani’s Il Corpo is the sound of something beautiful beginning to sour. Released in 1974, the soundtrack finds the Italian composer in familiar aesthetic territory, where jazz, funk, psychedelia and library music bleed into one another. Sunny music for shady people, it embodies the anything-goes spirit of Italian library music, spinning a parallel film from grooves, fuzz and atmosphere.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Transmissions :: Richard Thompson (2026)
aquariumdrunkard.description: Hippies, Thugs, and Heroes finds guitarist Richard Thompson sounding as savage, lyrical, and eloquent as ever. This week on Aquarium Drunkard Transmissions, we're pleased to welcome Thompson back to the show. If you dig Transmissions, there’s a pretty solid chance that you already know that he's one of the founding fathers of British folk rock, known for his work with Fairport Convention, Sandy Denny, his former wife Linda Thompson, Nick Drake and others.

mubi.title: Masao Adachi: Demystifying a Legend
mubi.description: Masao Adachi in 2025. Photograph by David Matthew Davis. Masao Adachi is a filmmaker whose reputation well and truly proceeds him. Born in 1939 in Kyushu, Japan, he moved to Tokyo to attend Nihon University, coming of age during the turbulent protests against the renewal of the mutual security treaty between Japan and the United States in 1959–60. He started making films with a student group and soon emerged as one of the leading figures in the burgeoning underground cinema scene. In the mid-1960s, Adachi became involved with the sexploitation industry, writing and directing several striking examples of the genre for Koji Wakamatsu’s production company. He was also collaborating with major…

Disney—Walt’s nephew and the vice chairman of the company’s Board of Directors—that he sent Mooney a note accusing him of “positioning Tinker Bell as a prostitute.” Mooney’s job was saved by the peacemaking…

W. Murnau completed work on his final German film and his most ambitious one to date, members of his crew compiled a scrapbook of illustrations and photographs that documented the making of that film, bound inside a prop Bible, and presented it to Murnau as a memento of the production prior to his impending move to Hollywood. Considered lost for many years, the Faust Bible was recently rediscovered and restored by the Cinématheque, and now MUBI and the Cinématheque have recreated this…

mubi.title: What the Image Hides: Tai Katō and the Art of Partial Vision
mubi.description: LOOKING THROUGH THE ROOM Blood of Revenge (Tai Katō, 1965). In Blood of Revenge (1965), Hatsue, a young woman bound by contract to a pleasure house, wants to see her dying father. Wearing violet, she bows low to the floor and begs Okatsu, who manages the house, for permission to leave. Okatsu reminds her that she has already been “bought and paid for” and is no longer free to leave on her own. The film’s director, Tai Katō, does not frame the plea as a simple exchange between two people. Hatsue is fully in view, but Okatsu sits deeper in the room, partly screened by translucent fabric. A man leans into the frame from the right. On the left, a woman is just visible in the shadows. She then…

With everyone behind her reduced to darkened figures, Floriane alone is lit up, as if she were living in a world of her own. The scene comes from Céline Sciamma’s debut feature, Naissance des pieuvres (2007), also known as Water Lilies . Floriane, captain of the synchronized swimming team, is the beautiful yet unreachable girl who mesmerizes the unassuming, slightly awkward Marie (Pauline Acquart) from the moment she watches Floriane and her team…

mubi.title: Know Thyself: Eric Rohmer’s “Élisabeth”
mubi.description: Éric Rohmer in Out 1: Noli Me Tangere (Jacques Rivette, 1971). In 1946, the prestigious French publishing house Editions Gallimard published a novel called Élisabeth by a man named Gilbert Cordier. No one had heard of this Cordier before, or knew anything about him, for the simple reason that he didn’t exist. “Cordier” was a pseudonym adopted by a young teacher of Latin and Ancient Greek from Tulle named Maurice Scherer. When Élisabeth was released to blanket disinterest, Scherer began to branch out from literature into film criticism, and, later, filmmaking. With each new endeavor, the pseudonyms piled up. If, in 1949, you were to pick up a copy of Bulletin (the in-house publication of…
